nameStory: The Red Flat Bark Beetle gets its name from its remarkably flattened body that allows it to slip under tree bark like a living pancake. This paper-thin profile is perfectly adapted for life in the narrow spaces between bark and wood, where it hunts for prey and feeds on the nutrient-rich phloem layer.
description: The Red Flat Bark Beetle is a small, dramatically flattened insect that looks like it's been pressed in a book. Its body is bright reddish-orange to rust-colored and thin enough to slide under loose bark with ease. These beetles are typically found crawling on or under the bark of dead poplar and ash trees, where they hunt smaller insects and feed on tree tissues.

idTips.label: Extremely flat body
idTips.description: Body is so remarkably thin and flattened it looks almost two-dimensional, like a beetle that's been squished but is still alive and moving

idTips.label: Bright red-orange color
idTips.description: Vibrant reddish-orange to rust-colored body that stands out against dark bark, much brighter than most bark beetles

idTips.label: Found under loose bark
idTips.description: Discovered when peeling back loose, dead bark from trees - they slip away quickly when exposed to light

idTips.label: Club-shaped antennae
idTips.description: Antennae gradually widen toward the tips, forming small clubs that are visible when viewing the beetle head-on

idTips.label: Smooth, shiny texture
idTips.description: Body surface appears polished and smooth, reflecting light and feeling slick to the touch if handled gently

habitat: Look for Red Flat Bark Beetles under the loose bark of dead or dying poplar, aspen, and ash trees in New England's forests. They prefer trees that have been dead for a while but still retain their bark, often found in mixed hardwood forests and along forest edges. These beetles are most common at higher elevations and in cooler, northern areas of the region.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under bark. This is when you're most likely to find them crawling on tree surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and active. Look for them hunting other insects under loose bark during warm days.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin preparing for winter, becoming less active but still occasionally found under bark. They start their remarkable cold-survival preparations.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under bark in a state of suspended animation, surviving temperatures that would kill most insects through special antifreeze-like adaptations.

funFact: Red Flat Bark Beetles are nature's ultimate freeze survivors - they can actually survive being frozen solid in winter by producing natural antifreeze chemicals in their blood, essentially becoming beetle popsicles that thaw out and walk away in spring!
confusionNotes: The extremely flattened body and bright red-orange color make this beetle nearly unmistakable - most other bark beetles are dark brown or black and much more rounded. If you find a bright reddish beetle that looks like it's been run over by a steamroller but is still walking around, you've found your Red Flat Bark Beetle.
compareHints: While there are no other Cucujus species in New England, Red Flat Bark Beetles are much more dramatically flattened than other flat bark beetle family members. Other species in the Cucujidae family are typically less colorful and not nearly as pancake-thin, lacking the extreme body compression that makes this species so distinctive.
